```js
expect(helper.getPage()).toBe(0);

Yes, here we're using `overrideStateWithoutTriggeringChangeEvent` to update the internal state without updating the UI since we do not want to change the page number in the URL ([RFC](https://github.com/algolia/instantsearch-rfcs/blob/master/accepted/infinite-hits-previous-page.md#detailed-design)).

I will add a comment to make it clearer.
I see! This is not caught by any tests though. We should add one.

We should keep the `.loadMore` button apart from this test, so I wouldn't test that there are two button there.

This "jQuery-like" way of testing is very fragile IMO because it would break easily if we were to change the order of the generated DOM, and we would lose the intent of the test again.

We could test it more declaratively and keep the snapshot:

- expect that `.loadPrevious` exists
- expect that it has the `.disabledLoadPrevious` class
- expect that it has the disabled prop

That would be my guess. I might be wrong though, let me know what you think.

```
Worth adding the assertion for the `disabled` class name.

We've implemented the `routing` but we always run it even when `showPrevious` is disabled. It means that previous implementation that use the widget have now their URL sync with it. We should only enable it when the previous button is present otherwise we might "break" their implementation.
We don't know whether or not we are on the last page but we do for the first since it's always 0.

body:
Not sure why (seems to be here from the first Instant Hits implementation https://github.com/algolia/instantsearch.js/commit/cdf867544a9acb9a4973f700fdc5230393ca3d51).

It was flushing the cache if you were reaching the first page. But even in the original implementation the widget had a weird behavior with this if you were using your browser to go back to previous pages: when reaching the first page the results list was emptied and only the last page was displayed.

This was even more problematic with the previous button, so I removed it.
Yep!
